title: Proxy for OpenAI Codex and Claude Code, use any LLM with those apps
author: dandaka
summary: this item describes a 'proxy' service that allows applications designed for specific large language models (llms), like openai codex or claude code, to instead use any other llm. a proxy acts as an intermediary, intercepting requests and forwarding them. this means if you have an application hardcoded to use a particular llm, this proxy can 'trick' it into using a different one without needing to change the application's core code. this is incredibly useful for flexibility and experimentation in full-stack development, mlops, and agent development. it allows you to swap in potentially cheaper, open-source, or custom models easily. when integrating llms into applications, think about how to design your system to be model-agnostic using an abstraction layer or a proxy like this.
why: increases flexibility, allowing you to swap LLMs in applications without code changes.

title: Show HN: We stopped feature-gating our open source BI platform
author: nikhelical
raw_text:
Hi HN, Nikhilesh here — c0founder of Helical Insight.We've been building Helical Insight for few years now as an open source BI platform, used for interactive dashboards, pixel-perfect/paginated reporting, embedded analytics, and now AI-powered conversational analytics.Today we've made a major change to our open source strategy.Instead of keeping advanced capabilities behind an Enterprise Edition, we've made the Community Edition feature-complete. It now includes AI analytics (bring your own LLM), embedding, SSO, multi-tenancy, row-level security, white labeling, scheduling, report bursting, dashboards, and pixel-perfect reporting. Source code present on Github.The only differences are:Community Edition includes a small "Helical Insight" branding on charts and exports that cannot be removed.
Community support is provided through our forum, while Enterprise customers receive SLA-backed support and can remove the branding.Our reasoning is simple: developers and organizations should be able to evaluate and use the complete platform instead of an artificially limited edition. We'd rather build our business around support, services, and enterprise SLAs than around feature gating.The project is primarily Java-based & react based, supports self-hosting, Docker, Kubernetes, and integration with multiple databases and identity providers. For AI, we lately introduced Python also.I'd genuinely appreciate feedback from anyone using Superset, Metabase, Redash, Lightdash, JasperReports, Pentaho, Crystal Reports, or SSRS.What would stop you from adopting an open source BI platform today? Happy to answer any technical or architectural questions.
summary: This news item announces that an open-source business intelligence (bi) platform, helical insight, has made its advanced features, including ai-powered conversational analytics, available in its free community edition. Previously, these features were reserved for an enterprise version. This change means that users can now leverage ai capabilities, such as bringing their own llm, directly within the open-source platform for tasks like generating insights from data through natural language. For you, this demonstrates a growing trend of integrating ai, especially llms, into traditional software products to enhance user interaction and data analysis. It also showcases how open-source projects are evolving to offer more powerful tools. You could explore how bi platforms use llms to provide conversational analytics.
why: Shows real-world integration of LLMs into products, enhancing data analytics.

title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness
author: Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih, Pinar Donmez, Babak Damavandi, Luna Dong
raw_text: Evaluating the factuality of long-form generations has focused predominantly on precision, measuring whether the claims a model makes are correct. The dominant decompose-search-verify pipeline catches incorrect claims well but says little about whether a response contains all the information it should. Measuring factual completeness, the missing half of factuality, is harder: it requires enumerating the full set of facts a complete answer should contain, and these facts rarely form a flat list. They often involve open-ended sets where coverage is what matters, ordered processes, and relationships among facts that a list of independent boolean checks fails to capture. We introduce a two-level meta-rubric framework for evaluating open-ended generation, and instantiate it as Gamut (Grounded Assessment of Multimodal Factuality), a benchmark for factual completeness in long-form generation. The framework rests on a two-level rubric representation: a structured meta-rubric captures the organization and importance of the required content, which is then mechanically compiled into a flat checklist of binary, machine-gradable rubrics that an LLM judge scores reliably. We construct 1,813 questions grounded in real wearable imagery across 10 diverse domains, each paired with an evidence-backed rubric verified by expert human annotators. Because the framework is modality-agnostic, we also release a text-only variant. Evaluating 14 frontier and open-weight models, we find the benchmark genuinely challenging (best score 58.7% from Gemini 3.1 Pro), highly discriminative, and robust to the choice of judge.
summary: this paper introduces a new way to evaluate large language models (llms) by focusing on 'factual completeness,' not just 'precision.' traditionally, we check if an llm's claims are correct (precision). however, it's also important to know if the llm has provided all the necessary information for a complete answer. this is harder to measure because defining what a 'complete' answer entails can be complex and isn't always a simple list of facts. the paper proposes 'gamut,' a benchmark to address this missing half of factuality. for your projects involving rag or genai, ensuring outputs are both correct and comprehensive is vital for building reliable systems. when you're evaluating an llm's output, try to think beyond just correctness and consider what important information might be missing.
why: crucial for evaluating LLM reliability and completeness in RAG and GenAI applications.

title: In-House LLM Serving at Netflix
author: sbulaev
summary: This refers to how netflix manages and deploys large language models (llms) within its own infrastructure, rather than relying solely on external cloud services. 'llm serving' encompasses the entire process of taking a trained model and making it available for real-time use, which involves challenges like scaling for many users, ensuring low latency, optimizing costs, and maintaining high reliability. for you, this is highly relevant to mlops and sde/swe roles, especially if you're interested in deploying ai at scale. understanding these real-world challenges gives you practical insights into the infrastructure and operational aspects of bringing generative ai applications from development to production. you could research open-source llm serving frameworks to see these components in action.
why: Crucial for deploying LLMs at scale, learning real-world MLOps.
